title: Equities, ETFs, Mutual and Index Funds
objectives: Explain what equity ownership confers (dividends, voting, residual claim) and compute dividend yields
Compute a fund's net asset value from its holdings and liabilities
Contrast ETFs and mutual funds on trading, pricing and cost dimensions
Quantify the long-run impact of expense ratios on terminal wealth
motivation: Most capital in markets is not one trader clicking one stock, it is pooled vehicles: ETFs, mutual funds, index funds. Understanding what a share entitles you to, how a fund's NAV is struck once a day, and why an ETF can trade all day near its NAV is prerequisite knowledge for anyone building portfolio or execution systems on top of these instruments.

blocks.text: A share is a slice of the firm

blocks.md: Common equity is a **residual claim**: after employees, suppliers, lenders and the tax authority are paid, shareholders own what remains, its profits, its assets, its losses. That residual position is why equity has unlimited upside and unprotected downside, and why it is the riskiest and historically highest-returning major asset class. Ownership also confers **voting rights** on corporate matters and, in many jurisdictions, pre-emptive rights on new issues. Income arrives as **dividends** when the board declares them, discretionary, not guaranteed.

blocks.title: Dividend yield on a hypothetical stock
items: You hold 200 shares priced at \$50.00: position value $= 200 \times 50 = \$10{,}000$.
The board declares \$0.40 per share quarterly: $200 \times 0.40 = \$80$ per quarter, \$320 per year.
On the ex-dividend date the share typically opens lower by roughly the dividend, value left the company with the cash.

blocks.title: Price is a claim, not the firm
blocks.md: A firm's market capitalisation (share price × shares outstanding) can exceed or collapse below the value of its factories and brands overnight. Equity price embeds expectations about *future* residual profits, which is why prices move on news about the future, not on accounting history.

blocks.text: Funds: pooling with a struck price

blocks.md: A **mutual fund** pools many investors' money into one portfolio and issues fund shares to each investor. Its price is the **net asset value** (NAV), computed once per day after markets close:

blocks.caption: NAV is the per-share value of what the fund actually owns, net of what it owes.

blocks.md: Example: a fund holds \$120m of securities and owes \$5m in accrued fees and payables, with 10m shares outstanding: $NAV = (120 - 5)/10 = 11.50$. Investors buy and redeem at that struck price plus or minus any sales loads, no intraday trading, which is by design: the fund does not need to hold trading liquidity, and investors transact at a fair end-of-day value.

blocks.text: ETFs: the fund that trades like a stock

blocks.md: An **exchange-traded fund** is legally similar, a pooled portfolio, but its shares trade on an exchange all day at market prices, bought and sold through a broker like any stock. What keeps an ETF's market price glued to its NAV is the **creation/redemption** mechanism: large authorised participants can exchange baskets of underlying securities for new ETF shares (or the reverse) at NAV. If an ETF trades at a premium, they create shares and sell them, pushing the price back; at a discount, they redeem. Arbitrage, not regulation, enforces the peg, which is why liquid ETFs track NAV within a few basis points while thinly traded ones can drift.

rows: Market price near NAV via creation/redemption

blocks.text: Index funds and the arithmetic of fees

blocks.md: An **index fund**, mutual or ETF, replicates a benchmark (say an S&P-style large-cap index) instead of picking stocks, so its main differentiator is the **expense ratio**: the annual fee charged against assets. Fees look tiny and compound brutally. Take \$50,000 invested for 20 years at a 7% gross return: with a 0.05% fee you effectively earn 6.95%; with a 1.00% fee you earn 6.0%.

blocks.title: Twenty years of fee drag on \$50,000
items: Difference: $191{,}684 - 160{,}357 = \mathbf{31{,}327}$, roughly 63% of the original investment, surrendered to fees.
Per-year the gap is less than one percentage point; per-career it is a car.

blocks.caption: The low-fee path: \$50,000 at 6.95% (7% less a 0.05% expense ratio) reaches about \$191,684 in 20 years. Reset the rate to 6.0% to see the 1% fee's cost: about \$160,357.

blocks.md: Finally, judge tracking quality with a simple metric: the **tracking difference**, cumulative fund return minus cumulative index return. A hypothetical ETF behind an index that rose 8.40% while the ETF returned 8.33% has a tracking difference of $-7$ basis points: fees, transaction costs and replication error in one number. For an index investor, choosing the cheapest, most faithful replication is the whole game.

guidedExercise.prompt: A mutual fund holds securities worth 480 (millions), owes 30 in accrued liabilities, and has 25 million shares outstanding. Compute the NAV per share. Then suppose the fund's market price (if it were an ETF) traded at 18.12, compute the premium or discount to NAV in percent.
guidedExercise.solution: NAV $= (480 - 30)/25 = 450/25 = \textbf{\$18.00}$. Market price 18.12 gives $(18.12, 18.00)/18.00 = 0.0067 \approx \textbf{+0.67\%}$ premium, a plausible small ETF premium that creation/redemption arbitrage would usually compress.

independentExercise.prompt: Two investors each put \$100,000 to work for 25 years at a 7% gross annual return. Investor A pays a 0.05% expense ratio (net 6.95%); investor B pays 0.40% (net 6.6%). Compute both terminal values and the fee gap. Then compute investor B's dividend yield scenario: a stock priced at \$48.00 pays \$2.40 per year, what is its dividend yield?
independentExercise.solution: A: $100{,}000 \times (1.07)^{25} = 100{,}000 \times 5.427432 = 542{,}743$. B: $100{,}000 \times (1.066)^{25} = 100{,}000 \times 4.942311 = 494{,}231$. Gap $= \mathbf{48{,}512}$ - a 0.4 percentage-point return difference costs about half the original capital over a career. Dividend yield $= 2.40/48.00 = \textbf{5.0\%}$.

commonMistakes: Comparing an ETF's market price to its NAV and calling small gaps 'errors', a few bps of premium/discount is normal, and it is arbitrage that closes it.
Computing NAV without subtracting liabilities (accrued fees, payables).
Ignoring expense ratios because '0.5% is nothing', they compound multiplicatively against every future year.
Treating dividends as free money: the share price typically drops by roughly the dividend on the ex-date.
realWorldApplication: ETF creation/redemption desks manage the NAV peg with baskets of securities; mutual-fund administrators strike NAV daily under accounting controls; fee competition in index products has cut expense ratios to single-digit basis points.
quantFinanceApplication: Portfolio systems price pooled vehicles via NAV feeds, compute tracking difference/error against benchmark indices, and model ETF premium/discount dynamics, a standard dataset in execution and arbitrage research.
summary: Equity is a residual claim with voting rights and discretionary dividends; yield = annual dividend / price (\$320 on \$10,000 = 3.2%).
NAV = (assets, liabilities)/shares; mutual funds transact once daily at NAV (here (120-5)/10 = \$11.50).
ETFs trade intraday near NAV because authorised-participant creation/redemption arbitrages away premiums and discounts.
Expense ratios compound: over 20 years a 1% fee vs 0.05% fee on \$50,000 at 7% gross costs \$31,327; tracking difference measures replication quality.

quiz.prompt: A fund holds assets worth 340 (millions) with liabilities of 20 and 16 million shares outstanding. What is the NAV per share, in dollars?
What principally keeps an ETF's market price close to its NAV?
options: The fund buys back its own shares every hour
Regulators set a maximum permitted premium
ETFs compute their NAV every minute
quiz.explanation: Authorised participants create shares when the price runs at a premium and redeem when at a discount; profit-seeking arbitrage keeps the market price hugging NAV.

quiz.prompt: A stock priced at \$48.00 pays a total annual dividend of \$2.40. What is the dividend yield, in percent?
Which are genuine advantages of index funds?
options: Guaranteed to beat the index every year
Low expense ratios and low portfolio turnover
Broad diversification in a single transaction
quiz.explanation: Index funds deliver the market's return minus small costs: cheap and diversified, but they fall exactly as hard as the index in drawdowns, by design.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
balance = 100000
for year in range(25):
    balance *= 1.066
print(round(balance))
quiz.explanation: Net of a 0.4% fee, 7% gross becomes 6.6%: $100{,}000 \times (1.066)^{25} \approx 494{,}231$ - the lesson's investor B terminal value.

quiz.prompt: A mutual fund can be bought or sold:
options: Once per day, at the NAV struck after the close
Only at a premium to NAV
Any time during exchange hours at market price
Only through an exchange order book
quiz.explanation: Mutual funds transact at end-of-day NAV; intraday trading at market prices is the defining feature of ETFs, not mutual funds.

flashcards.back: A residual claim on profits and assets after all other claims, voting rights, and discretionary dividends. Unlimited upside, unprotected downside.
Authorised participants swap baskets of securities for ETF shares (or vice versa) at NAV; arbitrage keeps the market price within a few bps of NAV.
Yield = annual dividend / price. Tracking difference = fund cumulative return − index cumulative return (e.g. 8.33% vs 8.40% = −7 bps).
